newsitem.title: USA: Lipreading helps even those who hear well-study.
newsitem.headline: Lipreading helps even those who hear well-study.

text.p: People who put on their glasses so they can hear better may have scientific support for their behaviour, according to research presented on Thursday.

British researchers reported in the journal Science that lipreading during face-to-face conversations markedly improves speech perception, especially in noisy situations. They said even people who hear well can understand what is being said better when they watch another person's lips move.

"Whilst we are usually unaware of the influence of these visual speech cues, they become obvious when watching a poorly dubbed movie, when the late or early onset of the speaker's lips actually hampers our ability to hear what is otherwise an extremely clear auditory signal," they said in a statement.

The movement of another person's lips, even in so-called pseudospeech composed of words strung together nonsensically, sends a message to the brain that helps in perception of the sound, the researchers said.

The lead investigator, Gemma Calvert of Oxford University, could not say specifically that the glasses-on-to-hear-better phenomenon was backed by this research but said in a light-hearted e-mail response, "perhaps this is the answer!"

In addition to helping in the study of language comprehension, the study was motivated by the observation that some some deaf schizophrenic patients report hallucinating "hearing voices" when they see people mouthing speech at them.
This suggested that the link between seeing and hearing may have implications for some psychiatric disorders.
